The question

Could virality skew web training data toward less reliable claims and contribute to language model hallucinations?

Full publication title

Training Data Velocity Bias: How Virality-Optimized Corpora May Explain Persistent Hallucination in Large Language Models

OverviewVisual explanationSelected pagesFull paper
Overview

Where a training corpus begins.

This preprint asks whether the speed at which information spreads can distort the material used to train language models. It proposes that engagement driven platforms amplify fast moving, less reliable claims, which may then be overrepresented in web training corpora and contribute to confident false answers. The paper defines a velocity bias measure, sets out a proposed Common Crawl and fact checking study, and describes five controlled model experiments to test the idea. It also considers how AI generated material could reinforce the pattern and proposes velocity aware sampling and weighting. The central link between virality in source ecosystems, training corpus composition and model hallucination remains a hypothesis. Its numerical values are predictions; the proposed studies await execution.

Key terms, in plain English
Corpus
The collection of material used to train a model.
Velocity bias
The paper’s proposed measure of how strongly fast-spreading content is represented in that collection.

What the paper proposes

  • Defines velocity bias as the relative representation of fast and slow spreading content in a training corpus.
  • Specifies a corpus study and controlled training experiments that could test the proposed causal link.
  • Proposes velocity aware corpus curation, sampling and training interventions.

Research status

The proposed corpus study and controlled model experiments have not been completed. The numerical correlation and bias ranges on page 7 are predictions extrapolated from prior social media research. The paper does not establish that web training corpora contain the proposed bias or that this bias causes hallucination. It acknowledges other possible causes and untested interventions.
